feedback: If the learner thinks the Roman system just needs a zero symbol added, point out that position must also carry value for zero to do its placeholder job.
Prompt the learner to connect the accountant's difficulty adding large numbers to the missing place value, not just unfamiliar symbols.
activities.intendedInsight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.
learnerActions: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed

feedback: If XLIV is read additively as 66, show that a smaller symbol before a larger one in an allowed pair (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract: XL = 50-10 = 40, IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44.

If the learner says the first symbol 'is in the tens place', contrast directly: in 44 position sets value, but in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add or subtract — Roman has no place value and no zero.
Reinforce the standard subtractive forms (IV, IX, XL, XC), reject invalid ones like IL, and treat IIII as a non-standard clock-face variant rather than the standard way to write 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.
learnerActions: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
